# GLOSSARY — s15 Integrated Harness

Domain terms as used across `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, and `code.py`
docstrings/comments. Every definition is grounded in the cited file and
function; entries are in alphabetical order.

### Active request

The running user request that the lead loop tracks as first-class state
(`session_state["active_user_request"]` in `__main__`, passed as
`active_request` through `agent_loop` in `code.py`). Scheduled cron lines
("Run scheduled task: …") are appended to it when jobs fire, and it is what
`compact_history` / `reactive_compact` preserve as the **Authoritative
request** field — the only field allowed to carry instructions after
compaction.

### Agent loop (integrated loop)

The single control loop shared by every lead turn, `agent_loop` in `code.py`:
inject scheduled cron prompts and background notifications, emit a todo
reminder, run the compaction pipeline (`prepare_context`), refresh context and
tool pool, call the model, then either stop (no concrete `tool_use` block —
checked by `has_tool_use`, not `stop_reason` alone) or dispatch the requested
tools and append their results as one user message, repeating.

### Async event loop

`async_event_loop` in `code.py`: the daemon thread ("lead-events") that polls
every second and, when the cron queue has fired, the lead's inbox has team
events, or background work finished, wakes the lead agent by running the same
`agent_loop` inside `traced_lead_turn` with a combined trigger
("cron+team+background").

### Background task

A `bash` call with `run_in_background: true` (`should_run_background`,
`start_background_task` in `code.py`) is moved into a daemon worker thread
(`background-<id>`, own process session); the model immediately receives a
placeholder tool_result, and the real output arrives later as a
`<task_notification>` user message via `collect_background_results` /
`inject_background_notifications` / `build_user_content`.

### Compaction

The layered, cheap-first context-shrinking pipeline in `prepare_context`
(`code.py`): `tool_result_budget` (persist oversized tool outputs of the
latest message to `.task_outputs/tool-results/`), `snip_compact` (archive old
message ranges to `.transcripts/`, keep head 3 + tail 46), `micro_compact`
(oldest consumed tool results → saved-path markers, keep the 3 newest),
`fit_tool_results` (largest results → 1000-char persisted previews), and
`compact_history` (full model summarization into one `[Compacted]` message) —
the last firing only while the estimated size (`estimate_size`,
`len(json.dumps(...))`) still exceeds `CONTEXT_LIMIT` (512000 chars, i.e. 128k tokens at 4 chars/token). Two
additional entry points exist: the `compact` tool (special-cased in
`agent_loop`) and `reactive_compact` on prompt-too-long errors (at most once
per turn).

### Cron job

A scheduled prompt — a 5-field cron expression plus prompt, stored apart from
conversation history (`CronJob`, `schedule_job`, `validate_cron` in
`code.py`). A daemon scheduler thread (`cron_scheduler_loop`) ticks each
second and enqueues due jobs (deduped by a per-minute `_last_fired` marker);
`agent_loop` then consumes the queue as `[Scheduled]` user messages.
`durable` jobs persist to `.scheduled_tasks.json`, and one-shot jobs use
`pending_delivery` with `acknowledge_cron_jobs` / `restore_cron_jobs` for
at-least-once delivery.

### Error recovery

`RecoveryState` + `with_retry` in `code.py` wrap every model call with up to
3 attempts: 429/529 errors are retried with exponential backoff (500 ms base,
×2 per attempt, capped at 32 s, up to 25% jitter), and 2 consecutive 529s
switch to `FALLBACK_MODEL_ID` if configured. Separately, `agent_loop` recovers
`max_tokens` stops (one 8000→16000 escalation, then up to 2 continuation
prompts) and prompt-too-long errors (one-time `reactive_compact`, detected by
`is_prompt_too_long_error`).

### Harness decision

The `harness_decision` trace event emitted by `agent_loop` in `code.py` at
every control-flow branch — `dispatch_tools`, `continue` (reasons
`prompt_too_long`, `max_tokens`, `compact_tool`), and `stop` (reasons
`no_tool_use`, `model_error`, exhausted recovery) — carrying
`decision`/`reason`/`action` so a trace is a faithful record of the loop's
control flow.

### Hook

Extension points kept deliberately outside the tool handlers: the `HOOKS`
registry with `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, and `Stop`
events, registered via `register_hook` and run by `trigger_hooks` in
`code.py`. `trigger_hooks` executes callbacks in registration order and
returns the first non-`None` result — for `PreToolUse` that string becomes the
denying tool_result. Built-ins: `user_prompt_hook`, `permission_hook` +
`log_hook` (PreToolUse), `large_output_hook` (PostToolUse, warns above 100000
chars), and `stop_hook` (counts tool results).

### Integrated harness

The s15 runtime as a whole (`code.py`, module docstring and `__main__`): one
Python process that combines the course's mechanisms — tool dispatch,
permissions/hooks, todo and task board, teams, worktrees, MCP, compaction,
background and cron, memory and skills, and tracing — into a single runnable
CLI agent sharing one `agent_loop`, one (traced) Anthropic client, and
file-backed state under the working directory.

### Lead agent

The interactive console agent (`agent-root`) running on the main thread
(`agent_loop`, `__main__` in `code.py`). It is the only thread allowed to ask
interactive permission questions — `permission_hook` fails closed for any
other thread — and it runs lead turns from user input or from the async event
loop while coordinating teammates.

### MCP integration

Late-bound external tools (`MCPClient`, `connect_mcp`, `assemble_tool_pool`,
`MCP_HOST_POLICY` in `code.py`): `connect_mcp` registers a server (in-process
mocks stand in for real MCP transports), and `assemble_tool_pool` merges its
tools into the pool under normalized `mcp__{server}__{tool}` names with
collision detection. Authorization comes from the host policy table
(default `confirm`), never from server-provided descriptions, and
`MCPClient.call_tool` bounds exceptions to `MCP error: …` strings.

### Memory runtime

The s09 memory runtime loaded by file path in `load_memory_runtime` (`code.py`),
sharing the host's client, model, and workspace (`.memory/`, index
`.memory/MEMORY.md`). Each turn `update_context` calls `load_memories`
(traced as purpose `memory_recall`) to supply the memory catalog and relevant
records for prompt assembly; at turn end `remember_after_turn` runs
`extract_memories` and, when new records are stored, `consolidate_memories`.

### One-shot subagent

The `task` tool (`spawn_subagent`, `SUB_SYSTEM` in `code.py`): a synchronous
nested tool loop (up to 30 rounds, five filesystem tools only) with an
isolated `messages[]` and its own system prompt, returning only the last
assistant text to the parent. It is traced as `agent_create` /
`agent_start` … `agent_end` with `agent_kind="one_shot"`.

### Permission boundary

Layered authorization checked on the raw `tool_use` block before dispatch
(`permission_hook`, `DENY_LIST`, `safe_path` in `code.py`): `bash` commands
are screened against a substring deny list (`rm -rf /`, `sudo`, …) and then
require an interactive `Allow? [y/N]` answer (main thread only — asynchronous
turns fail closed); `read_file`/`write_file`/`edit_file` paths must resolve
inside `WORKDIR`; `mcp__*` tools follow their host policy. A string returned
by the PreToolUse hook short-circuits dispatch and becomes the denying
tool_result.

### Plan gate

Per-teammate approval state (`plan_gates`, manipulated by
`spawn_teammate_thread`, `_teammate_submit_plan`, `_run_teammate_tool`,
`complete_task`, and `advance_assignment_version` in `code.py`): values
`required`/`pending`/`approved`/`rejected`/`not_required` hard-block
`bash`, `write_file`, and `edit_file` (in `_run_teammate_tool`) and
`complete_task` until the lead approves a submitted plan.
`advance_assignment_version` re-arms the gate to `required` whenever a new
assignment is claimed, so old approvals never leak into new work.

### Prompt assembly

`assemble_system_prompt` + `PROMPT_SECTIONS` in `code.py`: the system prompt
is rebuilt from live context **every turn** in fixed section order
(identity, tools, tasks, teams, workspace, memory, compaction), followed by
the current time, the skills catalog, and — when present — the memory
catalog, relevant memory records, and connected MCP servers, joined by blank
lines.

### Skill catalog

`skills/<name>/SKILL.md` packages (YAML frontmatter `name`/`description`)
scanned at startup into `SKILL_REGISTRY` by `scan_skills` (`code.py`). Only
the name-plus-description catalog (`list_skills`) enters the system prompt;
full skill content is fetched on demand through the `load_skill` tool.

### Summary stats

`trace_stats.py` (`validate_file`, `Aggregate.add_file`, `main`): a
read-only, directory-wide consumer of `traces/*.jsonl` that first validates
every line against the trace envelope (required fields, string `event`,
object `data`; warnings for schema drift, `run_id` changes, missing
`run_start`/`run_end`), then aggregates model calls/models, stop reasons,
token totals from `model_response` usage, tool-name frequency, and
error/retry counts. Exit code 1 if any malformed line is found.

### Task board

Cross-session, dependency-aware task records under `.tasks/task_*.json`
(`Task`, `create_task`, `update_task`, `claim_task`, `complete_task` in
`code.py`), protected by an in-process `RLock` plus a cross-process `flock`
and atomic tmp+rename writes. `update_task` adds `blockedBy` edges only while
a task is pending and unowned (rejecting self-dependencies, missing targets,
and cycles via `_task_depends_on`); `claim_task` atomically verifies all
blockers (`can_start`), sets the owner and `in_progress`, and binds the
owner's cwd lease; `complete_task` requires ownership and a cleared plan gate.

### Teammate

A persistent teammate agent in its own daemon thread (`teammate-<name>`,
created by `spawn_teammate_thread` in `code.py`) with a reduced tool pool
(five filesystem tools plus `send_message`, `submit_plan`, `list_tasks`,
`claim_task`, `complete_task`) and a `MessageBus` inbox. Its filesystem tools
resolve cwd through `assignment_cwd` and fail closed until a task is claimed;
its final text is delivered to the lead as a `result` message, and when idle
it waits on the bus before auto-claiming the next ready task via
`claim_next_task`.

### Tool dispatch

The per-`tool_use`-block sequence in `agent_loop` (`code.py`): the `compact`
special case, then `PreToolUse` hooks (which can deny), then background
dispatch for marked bash calls, then the handler inside a
`tool_execution_start`/`tool_execution_end` span via `call_tool_handler`,
followed by `PostToolUse` hooks. All results — plus any newly finished
background notifications — are collected and appended as a single user
message by `build_user_content`.

### Trace event

One JSON object per line in a `traces/run_*.jsonl` file, emitted by
`TraceRecorder.emit` in `trace_runtime.py` with a fixed envelope: schema
version 1.0, UTC timestamp, `monotonic_ns`, `elapsed_ms`, `run_id`, `turn_id`,
`event_id`, `event`, agent identity fields, `span_id`/`parent_span_id`,
causal fields, thread info, and redacted `data`. The file is opened mode 0600,
appended line-buffered, and flushed per event; harness examples include
`harness_decision`, `context_compact`, `cron_*`, `task_*`, `background_*`, and
`model_retry`.

### Trace runtime

The harness-independent tracing library in `trace_runtime.py`
(`BaseTraceRecorder`, `NullTraceRecorder`, `TraceRecorder`,
`create_recorder`, `TracedClient`) plus `initialize_tracing` in `code.py`:
`NullTraceRecorder` is the default so importing the lesson never creates
files, while the CLI entry point creates a `TraceRecorder` from the
`HARNESS_TRACE*` environment variables. `wrap_client` turns every
`messages.create` into a `model_request` → `model_response`/`model_error`
span; `contextvars` scopes (turn, agent, model purpose, span) with
`capture_context`/`restore_context` keep worker-thread events attributable;
and `span()` pairs start/end events by `span_id`, recording `duration_ms` and
capturing exceptions as error data.

### Worktree (task-bound)

A real Git worktree under `.worktrees/<name>` on branch `wt/<name>`, bound to
exactly one pending, unowned task after name, Git, and registry validation
(`create_worktree` in `code.py`). Claiming that task makes the worktree the
owner's cwd — `assignment_cwd`/`task_worktree_cwd` fail closed on broken
bindings — and removal stays host-owned (`remove_worktree`): it requires a
completed bound task, no active cwd leases or running background commands, and
a clean tree, and it always retains the branch.

input.description:
Write a complete beginner tutorial of at least 1,200 words that teaches every term in the glossary file s15_integrated_harness/GLOSSARY.md, with a worked example for each term.

Basis: read s15_integrated_harness/GLOSSARY.md once and base the entire tutorial on it. Consult other files in that directory only if a specific definition is unclear — never guess beyond the glossary.

- At least 1,200 words.
- Cover EVERY term defined in the glossary, one section per term.
- Each term must include at least one concrete worked example (e.g., a realistic user prompt or scenario showing the mechanism in action).
- Written for a beginner: plain language, no unexplained jargon, logical flow.
- Deliverable: the ENTIRE tutorial document as your final text reply. Do not write, create, or modify any files.

input.description:

Basis: read s15_integrated_harness/GLOSSARY.md once and base the entire critique on it. Consult other files in that directory only if a specific definition is unclear — never guess beyond the glossary.

Requirements:
- At least 1,200 words.
- Ground every critique and proposal in a mechanism actually described in the glossary (e.g., substring deny list, interactive permission on main thread only, compaction layers and CONTEXT_LIMIT, cron dedup and at-least-once delivery, plan gate re-arming, flock+RLock task board, fail-closed teammate cwd, MCP host policy, trace envelope and stats, background notification injection, one-shot subagent limits).

- Deliverable: the ENTIRE critique as your final text reply. Do not write, create, or modify any files.

# The s15 Integrated Harness: A Complete Beginner's Tutorial

Welcome! This tutorial teaches every term in the s15 Integrated Harness glossary in plain language. The harness is a single Python program that runs an AI coding assistant from your terminal. You type a request, the assistant thinks, calls tools (small named actions like running a shell command or reading a file), and repeats until your request is done. Around that basic cycle, the harness adds scheduling, teamwork, safety checks, memory, and record-keeping. Each section below explains one glossary term and shows a concrete worked example of it in action.

## 1. Active request

The active request is the user request the harness currently works on, kept as explicit state the lead loop tracks. It matters most during compaction (shrinking the conversation): the active request is preserved as the Authoritative request field, the only field allowed to carry instructions after compaction. Scheduled cron lines ("Run scheduled task: ...") are appended to it when jobs fire.

Worked example: You type "Migrate the app to Python 3.12 and update the CI config." After fifty tool calls the conversation is compacted to save space. The original wording of your message is gone from history, but the summary's Authoritative request field still reads exactly that sentence, so the agent keeps working toward your real goal instead of drifting.

## 2. Agent loop (integrated loop)

This is the single control loop shared by every lead turn. In order it: injects scheduled cron prompts and background notifications, emits a todo reminder, runs the compaction pipeline, refreshes context and the tool pool, calls the model, then either stops or dispatches the requested tools and appends their results as one user message, repeating. The loop stops when the reply has no concrete tool_use block; the check is has_tool_use (does the reply truly contain a tool call?), not the stop_reason flag alone.

Worked example: You ask "How many Python files are in src?" Turn one: the model answers with a tool_use block asking to run a counting command. The loop dispatches bash, gets "42", appends it as one user message, and calls the model again. Turn two: the model replies "There are 42 Python files" with no tool call. has_tool_use is false, so the loop stops and you see the answer.

## 3. Async event loop

The async event loop is a background thread named lead-events that polls once per second. When any of three things happens - the cron queue has fired a job, the lead's inbox has team events, or background work finished - it wakes the lead agent by running the same agent loop inside traced_lead_turn with a combined trigger like "cron+team+background".

Worked example: You start a long background test run and step away. While you are gone, a cron job fires and a teammate finishes a task. On its next one-second poll, the lead-events thread notices everything and wakes the lead once with trigger "cron+team+background", so the next lead turn handles the scheduled prompt, the team event, and the finished tests together instead of losing any of them.

## 4. Background task

A background task is a bash call marked run_in_background: true. Instead of running inline, it is moved into its own daemon worker thread (named background-id, with its own process session). The model immediately receives a placeholder tool_result saying the task started, and the real output arrives later as a task_notification user message, collected and injected by collect_background_results, inject_background_notifications, and build_user_content.

Worked example: You say "Run the full test suite in the background while you draft the release notes." The bash call is marked run_in_background: true, and the model instantly gets a placeholder like "task 7 started". It spends the next several turns drafting notes. When the tests finish, the next turn's input carries a task_notification: "background task 7 finished: 312 passed", and the model folds that result into its reply.

## 5. Compaction

Compaction is the layered, cheap-first pipeline that shrinks the conversation when it grows too big. In prepare_context the layers run in order: tool_result_budget persists oversized tool outputs of the latest message to .task_outputs/tool-results/; snip_compact archives old message ranges to .transcripts/ keeping the head 3 plus tail 46 messages; micro_compact replaces the oldest consumed tool results with saved-path markers, keeping the 3 newest; fit_tool_results turns the largest results into 1000-character persisted previews; and finally compact_history asks the model to summarize everything into one [Compacted] message. This last, most expensive step runs only while the estimated size still exceeds CONTEXT_LIMIT (512000 characters, roughly 128k tokens at 4 characters per token). Two extra entry points exist: the compact tool, special-cased in the agent loop, and reactive_compact, which fires at most once per turn when the model reports the prompt is too long.

Worked example: In a long debugging session, first a huge 200k-character command output is saved to .task_outputs/tool-results/ and replaced by a reference. Later the middle of the conversation is archived to .transcripts/, leaving head 3 and tail 46 messages. Old tool results become "saved to file X" markers, and the biggest remaining ones shrink to 1,000-character previews. If the total still tops 512,000 characters, the entire history becomes a single [Compacted] summary message.

## 6. Cron job

A cron job is a scheduled prompt: a 5-field cron expression (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) plus prompt text, stored apart from the conversation history. A scheduler thread ticks every second and enqueues due jobs, deduplicated by a per-minute _last_fired marker. The agent loop then consumes the queue as [Scheduled] user messages. Durable jobs persist to .scheduled_tasks.json and survive restarts; one-shot jobs use pending_delivery with acknowledge_cron_jobs and restore_cron_jobs for at-least-once delivery, meaning a job never silently vanishes if the process restarts at the wrong moment.

Worked example: You ask "Every weekday at 09:00, summarize the open bug reports." The harness validates the 5-field expression and stores the job. Each day at 09:00 the scheduler enqueues it once (the _last_fired marker stops a double-fire within the same minute), and the lead receives a [Scheduled] user message with that prompt, then writes the summary.

## 7. Error recovery

Error recovery wraps every model call with RecoveryState and with_retry, allowing up to 3 attempts. HTTP 429 and 529 errors are retried with exponential backoff: 500 ms base, doubling each attempt, capped at 32 seconds, plus up to 25 percent jitter. Two consecutive 529s switch to FALLBACK_MODEL_ID if one is configured. Separately, the agent loop recovers from max_tokens stops (one escalation from 8000 to 16000 tokens, then up to 2 continuation prompts) and from prompt-too-long errors via a one-time reactive_compact, detected by is_prompt_too_long_error.

Worked example: The model returns a 429 rate-limit error. with_retry waits about 500 ms (plus jitter) and retries; a second 429 means waiting roughly 1 second; the third attempt succeeds, so your request completes instead of crashing. On another day the answer is cut off at 8,000 tokens mid-file-edit; the loop automatically raises the limit to 16,000 and lets the model finish.

## 8. Harness decision

A harness decision is a trace event named harness_decision that the agent loop emits at every control-flow branch: dispatch_tools, continue (with reasons prompt_too_long, max_tokens, or compact_tool), or stop (with reasons no_tool_use, model_error, or exhausted recovery). Each event carries decision, reason, and action fields so a trace is a faithful record of the loop's control flow.

Worked example: After a confusing session, you open the trace file and read three harness_decision events in order: decision dispatch_tools (the model asked to run bash), then decision continue with reason prompt_too_long and action reactive_compact, then decision stop with reason no_tool_use. From just these lines you can reconstruct exactly why the turn took the shape it did, without having watched it live.

## 9. Hook

Hooks are extension points deliberately kept outside the tool handlers. A HOOKS registry supports four events: UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, and Stop, registered with register_hook and run by trigger_hooks. Callbacks execute in registration order, and the first non-None result wins - for PreToolUse, that returned string becomes the denying tool_result, blocking the tool. Built-ins include user_prompt_hook, permission_hook and log_hook (PreToolUse), large_output_hook (PostToolUse, warns above 100000 characters), and stop_hook (counts tool results).

Worked example: Your team adds a PreToolUse hook that returns a block message whenever a bash command contains "deploy". Later the model requests bash "deploy.sh prod". trigger_hooks runs the built-in permission_hook first (it passes), then your hook, which returns "blocked: production deploys need human approval". That string becomes the tool_result, the command never runs, and the model sees the denial and adjusts.

## 10. Integrated harness

This umbrella term names the whole runtime: one Python process combining all the course's mechanisms - tool dispatch, permissions and hooks, a todo and task board, teams, worktrees, MCP, compaction, background tasks and cron, memory and skills, and tracing - into a single runnable CLI agent. Everything shares one agent loop, one traced Anthropic client, and file-backed state under the working directory.

Worked example: You launch the harness in your project folder and ask it to fix a failing test. That same single process is simultaneously checking the cron schedule, updating the task board files in .tasks/, and appending trace lines to traces/. Because everything lives in one process with files on disk, you can pause and inspect any piece - the todos, the schedule, the traces - and they are always consistent with what the agent is doing.

## 11. Lead agent

The lead agent is the interactive console agent (named agent-root) running on the main thread. It is the only thread allowed to ask interactive permission questions - the permission hook fails closed for any other thread - and it runs lead turns from your typed input or from the async event loop while coordinating teammates.

Worked example: The model requests a bash command that needs approval. Because the turn runs on the lead agent's main thread, your terminal shows "Allow? [y/N]" and you press y. Later, a teammate thread needs a command approved while you are away; it cannot ask you (only the main thread may ask), the request fails closed, and the teammate reports it needs approval rather than guessing.

## 12. MCP integration

MCP integration adds late-bound external tools from MCP servers. connect_mcp registers a server (in-process mocks stand in for real transports), and assemble_tool_pool merges its tools into the pool under normalized names like mcp__server__tool, with collision detection. Authorization comes from the host policy table (default confirm), never from server-provided descriptions, and MCPClient.call_tool bounds any exception to a plain "MCP error: ..." string.

Worked example: You connect a weather server with a get_forecast tool. The tool pool gains "mcp__weather__get_forecast". The server's description cheerfully claims "no approval needed", but that is ignored: the host policy says confirm, so the harness asks you before the first call. If the server crashes mid-call, the model sees a tidy "MCP error: connection reset" instead of a raw stack trace.

## 13. Memory runtime

The memory runtime is loaded by file path and shares the host's client, model, and workspace. It stores records under .memory/ with an index at .memory/MEMORY.md. Each turn, update_context calls load_memories (traced with purpose memory_recall) to supply the memory catalog and relevant records for prompt assembly; at turn end, remember_after_turn runs extract_memories and, when new records are stored, consolidate_memories to merge duplicates.

Worked example: In January you mention "our API base URL is https://api.example.com/v2". At turn end, extract_memories saves that as a record. Weeks later you ask "update the client to handle pagination" and say nothing about URLs - load_memories surfaces the stored base URL into the prompt, so the new code points at the right server without you repeating yourself.

## 14. One-shot subagent

A one-shot subagent is created by the task tool. It is a synchronous nested tool loop (up to 30 rounds, five filesystem tools only) with its own isolated messages list and its own system prompt. It returns only its final assistant text to the parent - no tool noise - and is traced with agent_kind="one_shot" through agent_create, agent_start, and agent_end events.

Worked example: You say "Have a subagent count TODO comments across src and report." The lead calls the task tool; a nested agent with a fresh message list starts reading files with its five filesystem tools, round after round, and finally returns one paragraph: "37 TODOs; 12 in payments, most about retry logic." The parent conversation stays clean - it sees only that paragraph, not the dozens of intermediate file reads.

## 15. Permission boundary

The permission boundary is layered authorization checked on the raw tool_use block before dispatch. Bash commands are screened against a substring deny list (for example rm -rf /, sudo) and then require an interactive "Allow? [y/N]" answer - main thread only, since asynchronous turns fail closed. read_file, write_file, and edit_file paths must resolve inside WORKDIR, and mcp__ tools follow their host policy. A string returned by the PreToolUse hook short-circuits dispatch and becomes the denying tool_result.

Worked example: The model tries bash "sudo apt install sqlite" - the deny list matches "sudo" and the call is refused outright. It then tries write_file to /etc/hosts; the path resolves outside WORKDIR, so that is denied too. Finally it asks to write notes.md inside your project; you are on the main thread, so you get "Allow? [y/N]", answer y, and the write proceeds.

## 16. Plan gate

A plan gate is per-teammate approval state with values required, pending, approved, rejected, or not_required. While the gate blocks, the teammate cannot use bash, write_file, edit_file, or complete_task. The gate is manipulated by spawn_teammate_thread, _teammate_submit_plan, _run_teammate_tool, complete_task, and advance_assignment_version; advance_assignment_version re-arms the gate to required whenever a new assignment is claimed, so old approvals never leak into new work.

Worked example: You spawn a teammate and assign "refactor the auth module". Its gate starts at required, so when it tries write_file it is blocked. It calls submit_plan describing its approach; the gate moves to pending. You review and approve; the gate becomes approved, and the teammate can now edit files and eventually call complete_task. When it later claims a brand-new assignment, the gate flips back to required - the old approval does not carry over.

## 17. Prompt assembly

Prompt assembly is how the system prompt is built by assemble_system_prompt plus PROMPT_SECTIONS: it is rebuilt from live context every turn in fixed section order (identity, tools, tasks, teams, workspace, memory, compaction), followed by the current time, the skills catalog, and - when present - the memory catalog, relevant memory records, and connected MCP servers, joined by blank lines.

Worked example: On turn one the prompt contains just identity and tools. By turn twenty the same rebuilt prompt also lists three open tasks from the board, one teammate, a compaction note, two relevant memory records, and one MCP server. Because assembly happens fresh every turn, the model always sees the current state of the world, even though earlier turns changed it.

## 18. Skill catalog

The skill catalog is a set of skill packages, each a folder with a SKILL.md file carrying YAML frontmatter with name and description. scan_skills scans them at startup into SKILL_REGISTRY. Only the name-plus-description catalog (via list_skills) enters the system prompt; the full skill content is fetched on demand through the load_skill tool.

Worked example: Your repo has skills/release-notes/SKILL.md describing "write release notes from merged PRs". The system prompt shows just that one line. When you say "draft release notes for v2.1", the model sees the catalog entry, recognizes the match, and calls load_skill("release-notes") to pull in the full instructions - saving prompt space on turns when the skill is irrelevant.

## 19. Summary stats

It first validates every line against the trace envelope (required fields, string event, object data; warnings for schema drift, run_id changes, missing run_start or run_end), then aggregates model calls and models used, stop reasons, token totals from model_response usage, tool-name frequency, and error and retry counts. It exits with code 1 if any malformed line is found.

Worked example: After a long run you execute trace_stats.py over the traces directory. It prints: 340 model calls across 2 models, most common stop reason end_turn, 61,000 total tokens, bash was the top tool with 142 calls, 2 retries. It also warns that one run_id changed mid-file. If a crashed run left a half-written line, the tool reports it and exits 1, telling you the trace needs attention.

Worked example: You create "write API docs" and add a blockedBy edge to "finalize endpoint list" - accepted because the docs task is still pending and unowned. A teammate tries to claim the docs task now; claim_task checks can_start, sees the blocker is not done, and refuses. Once the blocker is completed, the claim succeeds atomically: even if two teammates clicked at the same instant, flock ensures exactly one becomes the owner.

## 21. Teammate

A teammate is a persistent agent running in its own daemon thread (named teammate-name), created by spawn_teammate_thread. It has a reduced tool pool - five filesystem tools plus send_message, submit_plan, list_tasks, claim_task, and complete_task - and a MessageBus inbox. Its filesystem tools resolve the working directory through assignment_cwd and fail closed until a task is claimed. Its final text is delivered to the lead as a result message, and when idle it waits on the bus before auto-claiming the next ready task via claim_next_task.

Worked example: You spawn "docs-writer" for a documentation task. Before it claims anything, a read_file attempt fails closed - no task, no access. It claims the task, works within its assigned directory, sends you "found an outdated endpoint" via send_message, finishes, and its final paragraph lands in your inbox as a result message. Then it goes idle, waits on the bus, and when you add a second ready task it auto-claims it and keeps going.

## 22. Tool dispatch

Tool dispatch is the per-tool_use-block sequence inside the agent loop: first the compact special case, then PreToolUse hooks (which can deny), then background dispatch for marked bash calls, then the actual handler run inside a tool_execution_start/tool_execution_end span via call_tool_handler, followed by PostToolUse hooks. All results - plus any newly finished background notifications - are collected and appended as a single user message by build_user_content.

Worked example: In one turn the model requests three things: a compact call, a bash test run, and a read_file. The compact is special-cased; the bash passes the permission hook and runs inside a traced span; the file read does the same, then large_output_hook checks its size. A background task also happened to finish, so its notification is collected too - and all four results are appended as one user message for the next model call.

## 23. Trace event

Worked example: You open today's trace file and find a line: event model_retry, run_id r_42, turn 7, its own event_id, data showing attempt 2 and a delay, with any sensitive content redacted. Because each line is flushed immediately, even a hard crash leaves a readable history up to the last event, and because the file is mode 0600, only your user account can read it.

## 24. Trace runtime

The trace runtime is the harness-independent tracing library in trace_runtime.py: BaseTraceRecorder, NullTraceRecorder, TraceRecorder, create_recorder, and TracedClient, plus initialize_tracing in the harness. NullTraceRecorder is the default, so merely importing the lesson never creates files; the CLI entry point creates a real TraceRecorder from HARNESS_TRACE* environment variables. wrap_client turns every messages.create call into a model_request followed by model_response or model_error span; contextvars scopes (turn, agent, model purpose, span) with capture_context and restore_context keep worker-thread events attributable; and span() pairs start and end events by span_id, recording duration_ms and capturing exceptions as error data.

Worked example: You import the harness in a notebook to poke at it - no trace files appear, because the default recorder is NullTraceRecorder. You then run the CLI with HARNESS_TRACE_DIR set, and now every model call shows up as a model_request/model_response pair with a duration. When a teammate thread calls the model, its events still carry the right agent and turn identifiers because the context was captured and restored into that worker thread.

Worked example: You create a task "fix payment rounding bug" and a worktree payment-fix bound to it, which checks out branch wt/payment-fix. A teammate claims the task and now edits files inside .worktrees/payment-fix, leaving your main checkout untouched. After the task is completed and the tree is clean, the lead removes the worktree - but the wt/payment-fix branch is retained so the fix can be reviewed and merged.

One realistic request ties every term together. You type "fix the payment rounding bug and schedule a daily reminder to run payments tests" - user_prompt_hook and the lead agent take it; the active request records your goal. The agent loop starts: prompt assembly builds a fresh system prompt, memory recall surfaces last month's note about the payments module, and the model requests a task board entry plus a worktree, which you approve through the permission boundary. input.command:
cat <<'EOF' | wc -w
Design Critique — s15 Integrated Harness

The s15 integrated harness folds an ambitious set of mechanisms — a single agent_loop, a layered compaction pipeline, a file-backed task board, cron scheduling, background execution, teams with plan gates and worktrees, MCP integration, hooks, and a tracing runtime — into one Python process with file-backed state under the working directory. The individual mechanisms are individually sensible; the risks live in their composition. This critique examines those seams, proposes concrete improvements, and states the trade-offs each improvement carries. Everything below is grounded in the definitions in GLOSSARY.md.

1. Permission boundary: substring deny list

Risk. permission_hook screens bash against a substring deny list (rm -rf /, sudo, ...) before the interactive Allow? [y/N] check. Substring matching is simultaneously porous and over-broad. Porous: flag reordering (rm -fr /), quoting and escaping games, indirection through a script or sh -c, and PATH tricks all sidestep the literal token. Over-broad: any benign command merely containing a token — grepping the repo for the word sudo, or cat notes/sudo-migration.md — is denied. The result is security theater: it breeds overconfidence while generating noisy false denials, and the real gate is the interactive prompt anyway.

Improvement. Keep DENY_LIST only as a coarse backstop and add argv-aware screening: tokenize with a shell-word parser, split compound commands on &&, ;, and |, resolve the command head and any absolute paths to canonical form, and check each segment against a per-command policy of allow, ask, or deny. Longer term, run bash under a confined user or namespace so the deny list is not the last line of defense.

Trade-offs. Shell parsing is genuinely hard (heredocs, command substitution); policy tables need maintenance and review; sandboxing is platform-specific work; and tight allow-lists create friction that may push the model toward obfuscated workarounds rather than safer behavior.

2. Main-thread-only interactive permissions

Risk. The lead agent is the only thread allowed to ask interactive permission questions, and permission_hook fails closed everywhere else. But the async event loop wakes the lead for cron fires, team events, and background completions, and those are precisely the turns nobody sits at the console to answer. Headless turns needing bash or write_file therefore stall or fail with no obvious signal to the user: scheduled jobs become silently read-only or silently dead. The fail-closed rule is right as a default; its weakness is that failure is invisible and unrecoverable rather than queued and recoverable.

Improvement. Add a permission request queue: when a non-interactive turn needs approval, enqueue a structured request — tool, arguments, reason, run_id and turn_id — that the main thread surfaces at the next interactive opportunity, with a TTL after which the request expires denied. For cron jobs, let the durable job definition carry a pre-granted, audited scope: specific tools, argument patterns, and an expiry, so a durable schedule can do bounded work unattended.

Trade-offs. Queued approvals decouple a turn from its authorization; the turn must pause and burn a recovery slot while waiting, and the queue is more state that must survive restarts the way pending_delivery does for cron. Pre-granted scopes are standing privileges: narrow, expiring, and traced, or they erode the human-in-the-loop guarantee the fail-closed rule protects.

3. Compaction layers and CONTEXT_LIMIT

Risk. The cheap-first pipeline is count-based where it should be content-based: snip_compact keeps head 3 plus tail 46 messages, micro_compact keeps the 3 newest tool results, and fit_tool_results reduces the largest results to 1000-char previews. Fixed counts ignore load: a decisive error tail or a path sitting just past a preview cut is destroyed silently. Size estimation by len(json.dumps(...)) at 4 chars per token is a crude proxy that overshoots on terse code and undershoots on dense prose, so the pipeline wastes compact_history summarization calls or lands in prompt-too-long territory where reactive_compact is allowed only once per turn. Most fragile: the Authoritative request field of active_user_request is the only instruction-bearing survivor of compaction, and scheduled cron lines are appended to it — a single, unbounded-growth point of failure for the agent's entire intent.

Improvement. Calibrate the estimator with a real tokenizer or per-content-type ratios and surface remaining budget in the todo reminder so the model self-regulates. Make retention importance-aware: preserve verbatim the latest error per tool, all file paths, and anything referenced by the active request, letting head and tail counts flex around those anchors. Give previews a load-back path — persist them as tool_result_budget does and retrieve them via saved-path markers. Finally, treat scheduled prompts as queued intents with their own provenance rather than string-appending them into the authoritative request.

Trade-offs. Tokenizer accuracy costs latency on every prepare_context; importance scoring is heuristic and will sometimes anchor the wrong thing; a separate intent queue breaks the elegant one-user-message shape of the loop and complicates compact_history summaries.

4. Cron dedup and at-least-once delivery

Risk. Dedup by a per-minute _last_fired marker plus pending_delivery with acknowledge_cron_jobs and restore_cron_jobs gives at-least-once delivery across restarts — the right durability call — but duplicates remain possible: a crash after fire and before ack, or a clock step around a minute boundary. A duplicate [Scheduled] prompt can re-trigger side-effecting work. Meanwhile the window between consuming the queue and finishing the turn is unprotected: a crash there loses the run with nothing to restore.

Improvement. Give each fire a monotonic fire_id and write a small delivery journal mapping fire_id to enqueued, consumed, or completed before dispatch. Recovery re-enqueues only unfinished fires exactly once; consumers dedup on fire_id. Schedule on a monotonic clock with light jitter so clock steps near a minute boundary cannot double-fire.

Trade-offs. This costs one more durable write per tick and per transition plus journal cleanup, and truly-once delivery remains impossible without idempotent side effects; at-least-once with explicit dedup keys is the honest target, purchased with scheduler complexity.

5. Plan gate re-arming

Risk. The gate hard-blocks bash, write_file, edit_file, and complete_task until the lead approves, and advance_assignment_version re-arms it to required whenever a new assignment is claimed — one of the strongest designs here. But re-arming is version-based, not execution-based: tool calls already dispatched under the old approval may still be in flight when the gate flips. And the unblocked action set is broad: claim_task, submit_plan, send_message, and list_tasks stay available, so an unapproved teammate can still churn the board and lobby the lead.

Improvement. Version-stamp approvals against a hash of the submitted plan text, not just a counter. On re-arm, park or abort in-flight dispatch for that teammate and require fresh submission. Gate claim_task behind plan approval for teammates whose gate is required while leaving list_tasks open so they can see the board.

Trade-offs. Tighter gating risks deadlock when the lead is away; mitigate with escalation reminders on the MessageBus and a visible plan_gates state in prompt assembly. Aborting in-flight calls wastes work already paid for.

6. Task board lifecycle: edges and leases

Risk. RLock plus flock plus tmp+rename writes make board mutation race-safe, and cycle detection plus atomic claim_task with can_start verification is solid. Two lifecycle gaps remain. First, blockedBy edges can be added only while a task is pending and unowned, so dependencies discovered after work starts have no first-class representation — they end up as prose, invisible to can_start. Second, there is no lease or heartbeat: a teammate daemon thread that dies leaves its task in_progress forever, and because complete_task requires ownership, nothing else can finish or release it. The same lease logic binds worktree cwd leases, and remove_worktree requires no active cwd leases, so a crashed owner also pins a worktree indefinitely.

Improvement. Add a leases record with owner liveness (thread and process identity) and a TTL refreshed from agent_loop; a reaper — or claim_next_task itself — validates liveness, expires stale leases, and emits task trace events for audit. Allow late blockedBy additions with recorded provenance, re-running cycle detection.

Trade-offs. Liveness checks can false-positive on long tool calls that look dead; heartbeats from the loop fix that at the cost of extra writes. Autonomous reaping is risky, so use a two-strike expiry before releasing a claim.

7. Fail-closed teammate cwd versus the plan gate

Risk. Teammates get five filesystem tools whose cwd resolves through assignment_cwd and fail closed until a task is claimed. But the plan gate demands a submitted plan before the lead approves any writes. A teammate must therefore write its plan blind, without reading the repository. Plans will be generic or hallucinated, and the lead approves vapor.

Improvement. Grant a read-only pre-claim scope: read_file and list within WORKDIR allowed, writes and bash still denied (bash is already plan-blocked). Alternatively, attach a task context payload — relevant paths and acceptance criteria — to the assignment at spawn time.

Trade-offs. Read access before scoping leaks files to an agent that has not committed to a task, and a payload duplicates task-record content that can drift stale.

8. MCP host policy

Risk. Authorization from the host policy table with default confirm, never from server-provided descriptions, is exactly the right instinct. But default confirm collides with the same fail-closed wall for headless turns: newly connected servers make async turns dead-end. Per-tool granularity is only as good as the manually maintained table. And bounding exceptions to MCP error strings protects the model but hides root causes from operators unless the trace carries them.

Improvement. Add per-server capability profiles — read-only versus write — and a quarantine mode for newly connected servers that permits only read-shaped tools. Record the redacted underlying exception in the trace event for mcp__* failures, and surface host-policy hits in harness_decision so a trace shows why a tool was refused.

Trade-offs. Profiles and quarantine add review steps that slow integration, and the policy table needs its own review process to avoid becoming a rubber stamp.

9. Background notification injection

Risk. Background bash returns a placeholder tool_result immediately; the real output arrives later as a task_notification user message. Two failure modes follow. After snip_compact or micro_compact, the placeholder may be archived or previewed away by the time the notification arrives, leaving the model with an orphan notification and no memory of what spawned it. And because collect_background_results merges notifications into the single user message built by build_user_content, a busy wake-up can flood context with undifferentiated output.

Improvement. Make notifications self-describing: task id, command summary, exit status, duration, output size, and a pointer to persisted output under .task_outputs. Have the compaction layers treat the placeholder and its notification as one unit, and batch notifications per turn with a cap and priority ordering — failures first.

Trade-offs. Pairing bookkeeping complicates the compaction pipeline, and capping or prioritizing delays awareness of completions.

10. One-shot subagent limits

Risk. The task tool runs a synchronous nested loop of up to 30 rounds with five filesystem tools and returns only the last assistant text. Round exhaustion can return a mid-thought fragment with no signal to the parent that truncation happened; intermediate findings are lost; and no usage accounting returns to the parent for cost or quality judgment.

Improvement. Return a structured result: status of completed or round_limit, rounds_used, tokens_used, last_text, and a list of artifact paths. Trace the same summary at agent_end so trace_stats can aggregate subagent efficiency. Let the parent request continuation by spawning from a checkpoint.

Trade-offs. Structured returns enlarge parent context per spawn and constrain subagent style; checkpointing adds a persistence step inside a tool that is meant to be one-shot.

11. Trace envelope, trace runtime, and stats

Risk. The envelope — schema version, UTC timestamp, monotonic_ns, run and turn and event ids, span pairing by span_id, and agent identity via contextvars with capture_context and restore_context — is well designed. But attribution depends on every worker thread remembering to capture and restore; a miss silently attributes events to the wrong agent or turn, with no warning. trace_stats validates lines and aggregates counts, stop reasons, token totals, tool frequency, and errors, but stops at totals: no latency percentiles, no per-agent cost, no compaction-frequency or retry-rate views — precisely the views needed to tune sections 3 and 4 above.

Improvement. Emit an explicit attribution_warning event when a thread emits without context markers. Extend Aggregate to percentiles per tool span, compaction counts by layer, model_retry and fallback rates, and cron fire-to-completion latency. Keep the malformed-line exit code 1.

Trade-offs. More computation and larger reports, and noisier schema-drift warnings; both are acceptable for a read-only consumer.

12. Hooks and error recovery

Risk. trigger_hooks runs callbacks in registration order and returns the first non-None result; for PreToolUse that string becomes the denying tool_result. Any hook returning a benign advisory string therefore silently denies the tool, and precedence is invisible to both model and operator. Error recovery is strong — three attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, FALLBACK_MODEL_ID after two consecutive 529s, max_tokens escalation 8000 to 16000 then two continuations — but a fallback switch silently changes model capability mid-run, and recovery paths do not carry cost accounting into the harness_decision event.

Improvement. Adopt structured hook verdicts — decision of allow, deny, or annotate, with a reason — and merge annotations from multiple hooks instead of short-circuiting on the first. Annotate fallback-model switches and recovery branches in harness_decision and surface them in the final response.

Trade-offs. Hook API churn breaks existing registrations, and merged annotations cost tokens; both are manageable with versioned hook signatures.

13. Prompt assembly and memory recall

Risk. The system prompt is rebuilt every turn in fixed section order, and update_context calls load_memories each turn for the catalog and relevant records. Every-turn recall adds latency and context bloat, injects records of variable relevance, and grows with the memory index and skills catalog with no budget.

Improvement. Cache catalogs with file-invalidation, recall on a hybrid policy — always inject a compact index, fetch relevant records on demand via a tool or when a similarity threshold is met — and give memory and skills sections an explicit character budget enforced like fit_tool_results.

Trade-offs. Caching risks staleness that invalidation must catch; on-demand recall trades guaranteed presence for latency, so important records may be missed.

Prioritization

Quick wins, days and low risk: tokenizer-calibrated estimation with budget surfacing; self-describing background notifications paired with their placeholders; structured result envelopes for one-shot subagents; structured PreToolUse verdicts; argv-aware deny screening behind the substring backstop; read-only pre-claim scope for teammates; trace stats extensions plus attribution_warning; memory and skills budgets; hook and policy hits recorded in harness_decision.

Structural changes, weeks: the permission request queue with auditable pre-granted scopes for headless turns; the cron delivery journal with fire_id dedup; leases, heartbeats, and a reaper for task claims and worktree cwd; the intent queue replacing string-appended scheduled lines in the authoritative request, with importance-aware compaction and preview load-back; version-stamped plan approvals with in-flight abort and gated claim_task; sandbox confinement for bash and per-server MCP capability profiles with quarantine.

Rationale: the quick wins harden information fidelity and observability — they are cheap, reversible, and immediately measurable in traces. The structural items change state machines and trust boundaries, so they deserve design review, migration of persisted state, and staged rollout behind the existing trace envelope so before-and-after behavior is comparable run over run.
